0.title: Using Our Tools Without Being Used by Them
0.overview:
Most people now carry a device that connects them to the whole world. It brings news, friends, music, maps, sermons and the entire Bible in one pocket. It also brings constant interruption, endless entertainment, pornography, comparison, outrage and the temptation never to be silent or alone with our thoughts. Many Christians sense that their phones are shaping them more than they would like, but they are not sure what to do about it.

The Bible does not mention smartphones, social media or artificial intelligence. But it says a great deal about the heart, the mind, attention, speech, community, rest and idolatry. These principles apply to every new technology.

Technology is not evil. Human beings were made to develop God's world, and tools are part of that calling. But tools are never neutral. They shape the people who use them. The question for Christians is not whether to use technology, but how to use it wisely, so that it serves God's purposes rather than our idols.

Five units: (1) Tools and the Heart; (2) Attention and the Mind; (3) Social Media and the Self; (4) Mastered by Nothing; (5) Embodied People in a Digital Age.

1.title: Tools and the Heart
1.overview:
Tools are a gift. God made human beings to fill the earth and subdue it (Gen 1:28). Developing tools, crafts and technology is part of that calling. In Genesis 4, the descendants of Cain developed livestock farming, music and metalworking (Gen 4:20-22). Noah built an ark. The skills of craftsmen built the tabernacle, and God himself filled Bezalel with skill for the work (Exod 31:1-5). Technology is a good part of human culture.

Tools can serve pride. At Babel, people used a new technology, baked bricks, to build a tower: let us make a name for ourselves (Gen 11:4). The problem was not the bricks but the heart. Technology can be used to glorify ourselves and to try to reach heaven without God.

Tools shape us. Psalm 115 says of idols: Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:8). We become like what we worship. In a similar way, we are shaped by what we give our time and attention to. Constant scrolling shapes us to be distracted. Instant answers shape us to be impatient.

Guard your heart. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (Prov 4:23). Technology enters the heart through the eyes and ears. What we watch, read and listen to shapes what we love and desire.

The right questions. Christians can ask of any technology: Does it help me love God and my neighbour? Does it make me more like Christ? Does it serve my calling, or distract from it? Does it master me? What does it cost me, in time, attention, relationships or purity?
1.theology:
Common grace: Unbelievers create many good technologies. God gives wisdom to farmers and craftsmen (Isa 28:24-29). Christians can thank God for medical advances, communication and knowledge, whoever developed them.

Neither fear nor worship: Some Christians fear all new technology; others embrace it uncritically. Both are mistaken. Technology is a tool under God, to be used with wisdom and gratitude.

Idolatry: An idol is anything we look to for what only God can give: identity, security, comfort, meaning. Phones and screens can become idols when they are where we turn first for comfort or meaning.
1.examples:
Then: The printing press, invented in the fifteenth century, made it possible to print Bibles and pamphlets cheaply. The Reformation spread rapidly through printed materials, and ordinary people could read Scripture in their own language. God used a new technology for the gospel.

Now: A Christian notices that the first thing he does each morning is check his phone, and the last thing each night is scroll. He decides to charge his phone outside the bedroom and begin each day with Scripture and prayer before looking at a screen. His mornings change, and so does his spirit.

A simple test: What is the first thing you reach for in the morning? What does that say about your heart?

verseByVerse.quote: And Lamech took two wives. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah. Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock. His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe. Zillah also bore Tubal-cain; he was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Among Cain's descendants, Jabal was the father of herdsmen, Jubal of musicians and Tubal-cain of metalworkers. Human culture developed rapidly, even in a fallen line. These were good gifts, though the same chapter shows violence growing alongside them (Gen 4:23-24). Technology advances, but the heart still needs redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the whole earth had one language and the same words. And as people migrated from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And they said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly." And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth." And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of man had built. And the LORD said, "Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them. Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech." So the LORD dispersed them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. And from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: People used baked bricks to build a city and tower, to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. God came down and confused their language. Technology used in pride and rebellion against God's purpose ends in confusion.

verseByVerse.quote: Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases. Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear; noses, but do not smell. They have hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk; and they do not make a sound in their throat. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist contrasts the living God with idols made by human hands. Idols have mouths but cannot speak, eyes but cannot see. Those who make and trust them become like them. We are shaped by what we trust and give ourselves to.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my words; incline your ear to my sayings. Let them not escape from your sight; keep them within your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life. Put away from you crooked speech, and put devious talk far from you. Let your eyes look directly forward, and your gaze be straight before you. Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure. Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The father urges his son to keep God's words before his eyes and in his heart. Guard your heart, put away crooked speech, let your eyes look straight ahead, ponder the path of your feet. Wisdom is a matter of what we let in through our eyes and ears.

1.reflection:
How is technology a good gift from God?

How has technology shaped your habits and desires?

What questions could you ask about a new app or device before using it?

Read Proverbs 4:23. What does it mean to guard your heart in a digital age?

2.title: Attention and the Mind
2.overview:
Attention is one of our most precious resources. What we pay attention to shapes what we love, what we become and how we spend our lives. Many modern technologies are designed to capture and hold our attention as long as possible.

Set your mind. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth (Col 3:2). Christians are called to direct their attention deliberately toward Christ.

Think on these things. Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things (Phil 4:8). This is a filter for what we watch, read and dwell on.

Turn my eyes. The psalmist prayed, Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways (Ps 119:37). Much of what fills our screens is worthless: trivia, gossip, outrage and noise. Some is worse.

Be still. Be still, and know that I am God (Ps 46:10). Stillness is increasingly rare. Many people never sit in silence, never have an unoccupied moment, never let their minds wander or pray. Yet stillness is where we often hear God most clearly through his word.

Deep reading. Scripture calls us to meditate on God's word day and night (Ps 1:2). Meditation requires slow, focused attention. Constant skimming and switching can weaken our ability to read deeply, including our ability to read the Bible well.

Practical steps. Turn off unnecessary notifications. Keep phones away during meals, conversations and worship. Set times of the day free from screens. Read Scripture from a printed Bible if your phone distracts you. Practise silence and prayer.
2.theology:
Love and attention: We give attention to what we love, and we come to love what we give attention to. Attention is a form of worship.

Distraction and the soul: Constant distraction can be a way of avoiding God, ourselves and our sin. Silence forces us to face what is really in our hearts. That is uncomfortable, but necessary for growth.

Stewardship of time: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil (Eph 5:15-16). Our time is a gift from God, and we will give account of how we used it.
2.examples:
Then: Jesus, even at the height of his ministry, would withdraw to desolate places and pray (Luke 5:16). Crowds pressed on him, but he made space for silence with his Father.

Now: A young mother finds she reaches for her phone whenever the children are quiet. She feels scattered and anxious. She decides to leave her phone in a drawer during the children's nap and use the time for prayer, reading and rest. She is surprised how much calmer she becomes.

A simple test: When did you last sit in silence for ten minutes without a screen?

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things. What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me—practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul gives a list of what to think about: true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, praiseworthy. Then he tells the Philippians to practise what they have learned, and the God of peace will be with them. Our thoughts shape our peace.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Believers have been raised with Christ, so they should seek and set their minds on things above. Their life is hidden with Christ. Our attention belongs to where our true life is.

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me, O LORD, the way of your statutes; and I will keep it to the end. Give me understanding, that I may keep your law and observe it with my whole heart. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I delight in it. Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain! Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways. Confirm to your servant your promise, that you may be feared. Turn away the reproach that I dread, for your rules are good. Behold, I long for your precepts; in your righteousness give me life! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist asks God to teach him, give him understanding and lead him. He prays, Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain! and Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things. Attention is something we must ask God to direct.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me." But the Lord answered her, "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Martha was distracted with much serving; Mary sat at Jesus' feet and listened. Jesus said Mary had chosen the good portion. Distraction was Martha's problem, not hard work. Sitting still with Christ is the one necessary thing.

2.reflection:
What captures most of your attention each day?

Use Philippians 4:8 as a filter. What would you stop watching or reading?

How could you build more stillness into your day?

What practical steps could you take to protect your attention?

3.title: Social Media and the Self
3.overview:
Social media can connect us with distant friends, spread good news and share the gospel. It can also feed some of our worst tendencies.

Seeking approval. For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Gal 1:10). Social media often rewards us with likes and followers, training us to live for the approval of others.

Performing righteousness. Jesus warned, Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them (Matt 6:1). Posting our good deeds, spiritual experiences or perfect family moments can become a way of seeking praise.

Comparison. Social media shows us the highlights of others' lives. We compare our ordinary days with their best moments, and envy grows. A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot (Prov 14:30).

Speech. Online, people say things they would never say face to face. Anonymity and distance make it easy to be harsh, mocking or careless. But let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up (Eph 4:29). Every word we type is still speech before God.

Outrage. Much online content is designed to provoke anger. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger (Jas 1:19). Christians should not be swept along by the latest outrage.

Good uses. Social media can be used well: to encourage friends, share Scripture, pray for others, support missions and maintain real relationships. The question is whether we use it, or it uses us.
3.theology:
Identity: Social media invites us to build and curate an identity. But a Christian's identity is given, not built: we are children of God, hidden with Christ (Col 3:3). We do not need to perform to be accepted.

Truth: Misinformation spreads quickly online. Christians should be careful to share only what is true, checking before passing things on (Prov 18:17). Spreading falsehood, even unknowingly, breaks the ninth commandment.

Privacy and wisdom: Christians should think carefully about what they share about themselves and others, especially children. Not everything needs to be public.
3.examples:
Then: Jesus taught that when we give, pray and fast, we should do it in secret, and our Father who sees in secret will reward us (Matt 6:3-6, 17-18). Secret godliness is safe from the hunger for applause.

Now: A Christian student realises she checks how many likes her posts get dozens of times a day and feels low when a post does poorly. She takes a month off social media. She discovers how much of her self-worth had come from it. When she returns, she uses it more sparingly and no longer counts likes.

A simple test: Before posting, ask: Why am I sharing this? Would I say this face to face? Does it build up?

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul is accused of trying to please people. He answers that if he were seeking human approval, he would not be Christ's servant. Living for the approval of others and living for Christ are incompatible. Social media constantly tests where we seek approval.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. "Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. "And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus warns against practising righteousness to be seen. Those who do so have their reward already: human applause. Instead, give in secret, pray in secret, and the Father who sees in secret will reward you. The hidden life of faith is safe from vanity.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul forbids corrupting talk and calls for words that build up and give grace. He warns against grieving the Spirit and lists bitterness, wrath, clamour and slander to put away. These instructions apply fully to what we write online.

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Human anger does not produce God's righteousness. This is a perfect rule for online life, where the temptation is to react instantly and angrily.

3.reflection:
Where do you seek approval most: from God or from others online?

How does social media feed comparison in your life?

How should Ephesians 4:29 shape what you post and comment?

What good uses of social media could you pursue?

4.title: Mastered by Nothing
4.overview:
Lawful but not helpful. "All things are lawful for me," but not all things are helpful. "All things are lawful for me," but I will not be dominated by anything (1 Cor 6:12). Many technologies are not sinful in themselves. But anything that masters us has become a problem.

Signs of being mastered. We are mastered when we cannot stop, when we feel anxious without our device, when it crowds out prayer, Scripture, work or relationships, or when we hide how much we use it. Gaming, streaming, scrolling and online shopping can all become compulsive.

Pornography. The internet has made pornography instantly accessible, and many Christians struggle with it. It is not a small issue. Jesus said lustful looking is adultery of the heart (Matt 5:28). It damages marriages, distorts views of sex and enslaves. But there is forgiveness and freedom in Christ. Practical steps such as filters, accountability and removing access are wise, alongside dealing with the heart. The Fighting Sin and Biblical Sexuality studies address this more fully.

Children and screens. Parents are responsible for what their children see and how technology shapes them. Train up a child in the way he should go (Prov 22:6). Wise boundaries, supervision and modelling good habits matter. Parents cannot teach what they do not practise.

Rest. Jesus told his disciples, Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while (Mark 6:31). Rest is a gift from God. Constant connectivity can rob us of real rest. A weekly break from screens, especially on the Lord's Day, can restore body and soul.

To God's glory. So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31). This includes how we use our phones and computers.
4.theology:
Christian freedom: Christians are free from legalistic rules about technology. But freedom is not licence. It is freedom to serve God and others, not to indulge ourselves (Gal 5:13).

Self-control: Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23). It is not mere willpower, but the Spirit's work in us as we depend on him and use wise means.

Habits: Small daily habits shape character over time. Changing technology habits may seem trivial, but it can have deep effects on the soul.
4.examples:
Then: Daniel and his friends refused the king's food in Babylon, choosing a simpler diet to avoid being defiled (Dan 1:8-16). They lived in a powerful culture without being mastered by it.

Now: A father realises he spends most evenings gaming after the children are in bed, and that his wife feels neglected. He confesses this to her, limits gaming to one evening a week and begins spending evenings talking with her and reading. Their marriage grows closer.

A simple test: Is there any technology you could not give up for a week? What does that tell you?

verseByVerse.quote: "All things are lawful for me," but not all things are helpful. "All things are lawful for me," but I will not be dominated by anything. "Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food"—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Corinthians used the slogan "All things are lawful." Paul agrees in part but adds two qualifications: not everything is helpful, and he will not be mastered by anything. Christian freedom includes freedom from compulsions.

verseByVerse.quote: "All things are lawful," but not all things are helpful. "All things are lawful," but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor. Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For "the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof." If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, "This has been offered in sacrifice," then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience— I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else's conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks? So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul again quotes the slogan and adds that not everything builds up. We should seek the good of others. Then he gives the great principle: whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Every use of technology can be measured by this.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Believers should walk wisely, making the best use of time. Rather than being controlled by wine, they should be filled with the Spirit, singing and giving thanks. What fills and controls us matters. The Spirit, not any substance or device, should govern our lives.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. And he said to them, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while." For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The apostles returned from mission, so busy they had no leisure even to eat. Jesus invited them to come away and rest. He cares about rest. Busy lives, including constantly connected ones, need deliberate times of withdrawal.

4.reflection:
What technology do you feel most mastered by?

What practical boundaries could help you use technology wisely?

How could you protect your children from harmful technology?

How could a weekly break from screens benefit you?

5.title: Embodied People in a Digital Age
5.overview:
God made bodies. Human beings are not minds trapped in bodies. God formed Adam from the dust and breathed life into him (Gen 2:7). We are embodied creatures, and our bodies matter.

The Word became flesh. God did not save us by sending a message from a distance. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The incarnation shows that presence matters. Jesus touched lepers, ate with sinners, washed feet and wept with friends.

Face to face. John wrote, Though I have much to write to you, I would rather not use paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete (2 John 12). Letters were good, but presence was better. Online connection is a gift, but it cannot replace being together.

The gathered church. Not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another (Heb 10:25). Online services can help the housebound, but they cannot replace the gathered body: singing together, taking the Lord's Supper, embracing, serving and being known.

Artificial intelligence. New tools can now write, answer questions and imitate human conversation. They can be useful for research, work and learning. But they are tools, not persons. They have no soul, no conscience and no relationship with God. Christians should use them wisely, check what they produce, never treat them as a source of truth equal to Scripture, and never let them replace human relationships, prayer or the work of thinking for ourselves. True wisdom comes from God: For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding (Prov 2:6).

The resurrection. Our hope is not to escape the body into a digital or spiritual existence, but the resurrection of the body and a renewed earth. The future is embodied, face to face with God and one another (1 Cor 13:12).
5.theology:
Presence and love: Love is shown most fully in presence: sitting with the sick, sharing a meal, embracing the grieving. Technology can support presence, but it is a poor substitute for it.

Human dignity: As machines become more capable, some may suggest that humans are no more than complex machines. Scripture insists that human beings are made in God's image, with dignity no machine can share.

Truth and discernment: In an age of deepfakes and misinformation, Christians must be people of truth, careful with what they believe and share, testing everything (1 Thess 5:21).
5.examples:
Then: Paul longed to see the Christians in Rome face to face: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you (Rom 1:11). Even the apostle who wrote so many letters knew that presence mattered.

Now: A church that moved its services online during a crisis found that some members never returned in person. The elders visit each one, explaining why the gathered church matters. Many come back and rediscover the joy of worshipping together. Those who cannot come are visited regularly.

A simple test: Are your closest relationships mostly online or face to face? What could you do to be more present with people?

verseByVerse.quote: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. (John bore witness about him, and cried out, "This was he of whom I said, 'He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.'") For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. We have seen his glory, full of grace and truth. No one has ever seen God, but the only Son has made him known. God's ultimate communication was not a message but a person, present in a body. Presence is at the heart of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Though I have much to write to you, I would rather not use paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John has much to write, but he prefers to visit and speak face to face, so that their joy may be complete. Written communication had its place, but presence completed joy. The same is true of digital communication today.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful. And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Believers are to hold fast their hope, stir one another up to love and good works, and not neglect meeting together. Gathering is the context for mutual encouragement. Online connection cannot fully replace the physical gathering of God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you, making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding; yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures, then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The father urges his son to receive his words, treasure his commands and seek wisdom like hidden treasure. Then he will understand the fear of the LORD, for the LORD gives wisdom. True wisdom comes from God, not from any human or machine.

5.reflection:
Why does the incarnation show that presence matters?

How can online connection support, but not replace, the gathered church?

How should Christians use artificial intelligence wisely?

How could you be more physically present with family, friends and church?
